questions.stem: The Japanese national holiday Keiro No Hi, which Levy observed while living in Tokyo, translates to what?
According to the study Levy cites, older Japanese men, who are treated "like rock stars in their country," were found to have higher levels of what compared with their European counterparts?
In Levy's study of residents of Oxford, Ohio, what was the single most important factor in determining longevity?
options: How people thought about and approached the idea of old age

questions.stem: Levy notes that for the first time in human history, there are more people in the world over the age of sixty-four than under what age?
What is the name of the framework Levy developed to explain how culture-based age stereotypes "get under our skin" and affect health?
Which of the following is NOT one of the four mechanisms of stereotype embodiment theory?
options: Age stereotypes increase in power as they become more self-relevant
Age stereotypes are internalized from society starting in childhood
Age stereotypes are inherited genetically from one's parents

questions.stem: According to Levy, infants as young as what age distinguish and sort faces by age?
Through the biological pathway, Levy's team found that negative age beliefs can increase which two biological markers of stress?
According to Levy, approximately what percentage of our health is due to genes?
When Levy asked people in China to name the first words or phrases that came to mind to describe an old person, what was the most common response?
In what year did the term "senior moment" first appear in print?
According to Levy, which type of memory, such as recalling the possible colors of an apple, tends to improve in later life?
In Levy's cross-cultural memory study, which group of older participants held the most-positive age beliefs and performed best across all memory tasks?
What sixty-thousand-word epic poem did retired actor John Basinger memorize, beginning when he was close to sixty?

Using data from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, Levy found that people who held positive age beliefs at the outset had how much better memory scores in old age than peers with negative age beliefs?
Neuroscientist Daniel Levitin says that "you want a 70-year-old radiologist reading [your x-ray], not a 30- year-old one" because which ability improves past age sixty?
Songlines, through which elders preserve and pass down knowledge of plants, animals, and maps of the land, belong to which culture?
Sister Madonna Buder, who has completed over 350 triathlons since 1982, is known by what nickname?
In Levy's month-long subliminal priming study, the physical improvement of participants exposed to positive age beliefs was similar to what?
options: One week of daily physical therapy
Three months of strength training twice a week
Two years of weekly yoga classes
Six months of exercising four times a week

questions.stem: When geriatrician Tom Gill surveyed older participants at monthly intervals, what percentage showed a complete recovery within one year of their initial disability episode?
In the New Haven study, participants holding positive age stereotypes had what greater likelihood of complete recovery from severe disability than those with negative age stereotypes?
In 1901, Dr. Alois Alzheimer began caring for which patient, whose autopsied brain revealed the amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles of the disease that now bears his name?
According to the research Levy cites, dementia was found to be how many times more common in the US than in India?
Among participants carrying the APOE 4 gene, those with positive age beliefs were how much less likely to develop dementia than those with negative age beliefs?
In the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, the hippocampi of people with negative age beliefs shrank how much faster than those of people with positive age beliefs?
Maggie Kuhn, who said "Old age is an excellent time for outrage," founded which antiageism activist group?
Over a thirty-year period, older participants with negative age beliefs showed a 44 percent increase in which stress hormone, while those with positive age beliefs showed a 10 percent decline?
Which founder of psychoanalysis discouraged therapists from treating older patients, arguing that people "near or above the age of 50" are "no longer educable"?
What term describes therapists' low expectations for older patients' improvement?
According to Levy, what percentage of mental health providers do not accept older patients who rely on Medicare?
Zimbabwean psychiatrist Dixon Chibanda's Friendship Bench program trains which group to provide talk therapy in their communities?
In the Ohio Longitudinal Study on Aging and Retirement, participants with the most-positive views of aging lived, on average, how much longer than those with the most-negative views?
Levy uses which animal as an analogy to show that environment can overcome genes, since individuals with identical genes can live five times longer depending on how they are treated and fed?
options: Lab mice raised in enriched cages

questions.stem: Which Japanese term, similar to the French "raison d'-tre," Levy offers as an expression of the will to live?
Stanford's James Fries uses what term to describe the growing number of years free of illness as humans live longer?
In Levy's New Haven hearing study, older participants with the most-negative age beliefs had what greater hearing decline over the next three years than those with the most-positive age beliefs?
According to Levy, older musicians are how much better than nonmusicians at hearing speech in noisy environments?
The German term "Alterstil," used by art historians and creativity researchers, refers to what?
options: An art movement that celebrated youth
The decline in artistic quality that comes with age
An old-age style marked by changes in technique, affective tone, and subject matter
A painting technique developed by Michelangelo

questions.stem: Who coined the term "ageism" in 1969 during an interview with reporter Carl Bernstein?

Using the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, Levy's team found that younger people who assimilated more-negative age stereotypes were how much more likely to have a heart attack or other cardiovascular event after turning sixty?

In a systematic review of how ageism impacts older persons' health, Levy's team found that in what percentage of studies on health-care access did providers discourage or deny older patients access to certain treatments?
Levy and her colleagues estimated that the health costs resulting from ageism in the US total how much per year?
Which limitation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) of 1967 does Levy point out?
options: It applies only to government employees
It applies only to workers over the age of seventy-five
It allows unlimited punitive damages, which overwhelms the courts
It applies only to people who already have jobs, not to job seekers

questions.stem: In Levy's ABC method for shifting to an age-thriving mindset, what do the letters A, B, and C stand for?
What term describes speaking to older people with simplified language, a singsong cadence, and a louder-than-normal voice?
The "Scully effect," named after the fictional FBI scientist Dana Scully on The X-Files, illustrates what point Levy makes about role models?
options: Positive role models can actually change behavior, such as girls who watched her being more likely to enter a scientific field
Older viewers identify more strongly with young characters than with old ones
Television viewers adopt negative age stereotypes from crime dramas
Fictional role models have no measurable effect on real behavior

questions.stem: Levy identifies three stages that could lead to the formation of an age liberation movement. What are they?
Research by Damon Centola's team at the University of Pennsylvania suggests that social tipping points can occur when what percentage of the population decides it is time to change?
At a United Nations working group, Levy learned that what percentage of older people in low- and middle-income countries reported they could not obtain needed health care because of their age?
In the Afterword, Levy describes a town where "ageism does not exist," home to the Greensboro Ladies' Walking Society. Where is this town?
After the grocery store owner told Grandma Horty that "old people fall down all the time," how did her behavior change over the following days?
options: She sued the store owner for negligence
She stopped trusting herself to drive and asked Levy to take her to a hair appointment
She moved into an assisted-living facility
She began a daily exercise program to prove him wrong

questions.stem: A hospital gives physicians two identical case files that differ only in the patient's age (45 vs. 80). The physicians recommend aggressive treatment far more often for the 45-year-old. Based on Levy's discussion, this pattern is best described as what?
options: Confirmation bias on the part of the patients
Sound clinical judgment, since the case files show different likelihoods of recovery
Structural and implicit age bias, since doctors are less likely to recommend treatment for older patients with identical symptoms and prognosis
Stereotype embodiment, since the doctors are internalizing beliefs about their own aging

questions.stem: When Levy pulled a muscle early in a 5K charity race, she instinctively blamed her age. What did her family point out was the real cause?
options: She had a pre-existing knee injury
She had arrived late and skipped her warm-up
She was wearing the wrong running shoes
She had not trained for the race

questions.stem: At age 25, Maria misplaces her car keys and thinks nothing of it. At age 75, the same lapse makes her worry she is becoming senile. Which mechanism of stereotype embodiment theory (SET) does this illustrate?
options: Self-relevance: age stereotypes gain power as they come to apply to oneself
The biological pathway through stress hormones
Internalization across the life span starting in childhood

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man stops taking his prescribed blood pressure medication and quits his walking routine because "decline is inevitable at my age anyway." According to SET, which pathway is his negative age belief acting through?
A woman writes to Levy, "Frankly I feel ashamed to be old... because society tells me it is shameful." Her lowered self-esteem is an example of which SET pathway?
Carl Reiner and Mel Brooks expressed positive age beliefs decades before they were old through which famous comedy routine?
options: "If You're Not in the Obit, Eat Breakfast"

questions.stem: Retired Apple engineer JK Scheinberg, who led the project that moved Apple's operating system to Intel, experienced ageism when he applied for what job?
options: A part-time position at the Apple Store's Genius Bar
Chief technology officer at a start-up
A teaching position at a community college

questions.stem: Why does the American Deaf community tend to hold positive age beliefs, according to Levy?
options: Over 90 percent of Deaf individuals are born to hearing parents, so young Deaf people form strong ties with older Deaf role models
Sign language has no words for negative age stereotypes
Deaf elders are required by tradition to lead community organizations
Deaf communities have no exposure to television of any kind

questions.stem: A researcher wants to show that culture, not language, explains differences in older adults' memory. Following Levy's study design, why should she include BOTH Deaf American and mainland Chinese participants rather than just one of these groups?
options: Both groups have identical diets, which controls for nutrition
Both groups have the same average age
Both groups speak the same language
Their only shared factor is positive age beliefs, which rules out alternative explanations such as signing or pictogram-based language

questions.stem: What memorization technique, learned from working with the National Theater for the Deaf, did John Basinger use to memorize Paradise Lost?
options: Associating each line with a musical note
Adding natural gestures to make the text physical and visual
Writing each line one hundred times

questions.stem: Anthropologist Margaret Mead wrote that "the continuity of all cultures depends on the living presence of" what?
Wilhelmina Delco, who took up swimming at age eighty, had earlier made history in what way?
options: She was the first woman to swim the English Channel
She was the oldest person to win an Olympic medal
She became the first Black person elected to public office in Austin, Texas
She founded the Gray Panthers' Texas chapter

questions.stem: A critic argues that Levy's functional health finding is backwards: healthier people simply develop more positive age beliefs. How did Levy and statistician Marty Slade address this?
options: They excluded all participants with any health problems
They conceded the critic's point and dropped the finding
They tested whether baseline functional health predicted later age beliefs (it did not) and compared participants with the same starting health scores
They relied only on participants' self-reports of health

questions.stem: A senior center wants to use positive age priming to improve residents' walking and balance. Based on Levy's research, which design is most likely to produce lasting gains?
options: One ten-minute session on the first day only
Repeated priming sessions at regular intervals (e.g., weekly for a month), since a single session's effect fades after about an hour
Daily sessions using random letters instead of age-related words
A single session that uses negative age words to motivate residents

questions.stem: A researcher surveys older adults once a year and concludes that older people rarely recover from disability. Based on Tom Gill's work, what is the main flaw in this design?
options: The survey should have included only people under seventy
Disability cannot be measured in older adults
Yearly surveys miss brief episodes of disability and recovery; monthly surveys showed most older people fully recover
Older adults cannot accurately report their own health

questions.stem: Which Oscar-winning actor, in his seventies, recovered from a severe car crash and went on to star in dozens more films, including action movies featuring older heroes?

In a debate on allocating limited resources to "patients with the greatest likelihood of long-term survival," a speaker assumes that older patients have poor recovery prospects. Which finding from Levy best challenges this assumption?
options: Older adults with negative age beliefs exercise less
Older adults remember semantic information better than young adults
Most older people prefer not to be hospitalized
Older adults with positive age beliefs had a 44 percent greater likelihood of complete recovery from severe disability

questions.stem: Amy, a retired bookkeeper born in Jamaica and enrolled in the A4 study, is notable for what reason?
options: She was diagnosed with Alzheimer's but fully recovered
She has elevated amyloid plaque in her brain but no cognitive symptoms of Alzheimer's
She developed dementia despite positive age beliefs
She carries the protective APOE 2 gene

questions.stem: Retired pediatrician Jonas recalls that his university had to do what when he retired, because of his accumulated knowledge and diagnostic ability?
options: Hire two younger doctors to replace him
Name a teaching award after him

questions.stem: Two 70-year-olds both lack the protective APOE 2 gene. One holds positive age beliefs; the other holds negative ones. Based on Levy's findings, what can be predicted about the one with positive age beliefs?
options: Their dementia risk is about the same as that of people born with APOE 2, so age beliefs act like a "cultural 2 variant"
Their dementia risk is the same as the person with negative age beliefs, because genes are destiny
They are guaranteed never to develop dementia
They will develop dementia faster because of higher stress

questions.stem: Why might positive age beliefs help a person with Alzheimer's biomarkers avoid clinical symptoms, according to Levy?
options: Positive age beliefs change a person's APOE gene variant
Positive age beliefs dissolve amyloid plaques directly
Positive age beliefs make people avoid medical testing
Positive age beliefs buffer stress, and stress boosts brain inflammation that accelerates neurological disease

questions.stem: What anecdote about Freud's mother, Amalia, does Levy relate to suggest the source of Freud's negative age beliefs?
options: She refused to let Freud treat any patients over fifty
At ninety she declined a beautiful shawl because it would "make her look too old"
She moved into a nursing home against her will
She hid her true age from her children her whole life

questions.stem: When psychiatrist Dan Plotkin wanted to take on a seventy-three-year-old patient ("JF") for his psychoanalytic training, what happened?
options: He was required to treat her only with medication
His supervisors rejected her because of her age, but he appealed, and she benefited greatly from therapy
She was transferred to a geriatric specialist
She refused therapy because she felt too old to change

questions.stem: A 74-year-old patient presents with depression. Her doctor says it is "a normal part of aging" and prescribes medication only. Based on Levy's discussion, what would be the better approach?
options: Accept the depression as normal aging and do nothing
Increase the medication dose instead of adding therapy
Refer her to a nursing home
Treat the depression as treatable and combine medication with talk therapy, which is more effective and cost-effective in the long term

questions.stem: A rural region has very few psychiatrists and no funding for new mental health workers. Applying Dixon Chibanda's model, what would be the most practical solution?
options: Wait until enough psychiatrists can be recruited from cities
Require patients to travel to the nearest city hospital
Prescribe antidepressants to everyone who screens positive
Train older community members, such as grandmothers, to deliver structured talk therapy in the community

questions.stem: Which classic Ingmar Bergman film, about a 76-year-old physician who gains insight into his life, does Levy show her Health and Aging class (following Erik Erikson's example)?
How did Levy discover a way to find out which Ohio Longitudinal Study participants had died?
options: The study's director had secretly recorded deaths
At a conference, a man handed her a ruler printed with "NDI," the National Death Index

questions.stem: In Levy's experiment, older participants were primed with age stereotypes and then asked whether they would accept an expensive treatment with a 75 percent chance of survival. What would you predict for an older participant primed with negative age stereotypes?
options: They would be more likely to reject the life-prolonging treatment
They would be more likely to accept the treatment
Priming would have no effect because the scenario is hypothetical
They would respond the same as younger participants

questions.stem: During COVID-19, a hospital notices that older patients with negative age beliefs are more likely to refuse admission. For a debate on allocating care by "likelihood of survival," why does Levy's finding matter?
options: It shows younger patients' age beliefs determine their treatment choices
Patients' own age beliefs can shape whether they seek treatment, so survival outcomes partly reflect beliefs rather than biology alone
It proves older patients should never be hospitalized
It shows hospitalization does not affect survival

questions.stem: In Levy's longevity equation L = (P, E), where do age beliefs fit?
options: They are part of the person's genes (P) only
They start in the environment (E) and then become absorbed by the person (P)
They belong only to the environment (E) and never affect the person
They are a separate variable unrelated to P or E

questions.stem: When the mayor of Kane Tanaka's town brought her a cake shaped like her favorite board game, what game was it?
Chilean ear surgeon Marcos Goycoolea found that older residents of which island heard better than those who had lived on the South American mainland?

In a study, participants primed with age stereotypes read about a 73-year-old woman who imagines that a crumpled napkin looks like an animal. How would a participant primed with negative age stereotypes most likely interpret her daydream?
A 65-year-old asks how to protect her hearing as she ages. Based on Nina Kraus's research described by Levy, what activity would be a reasonable recommendation?
options: Start making music, since beginning to play or sing even in later life benefits the brain and hearing
Avoid all music to rest the ears
Only listen to music through headphones at high volume
Wait until hearing loss begins before taking action

questions.stem: Choreographer Liz Lerman won a MacArthur "genius award" and founded which dance company known for its intergenerational dancers?
What contrast does Levy draw about the response to Hurricane Katrina?
options: Older people were evacuated first, before children
Nursing homes were the first buildings to be rebuilt
Hospitals refused to admit anyone under sixty-five
Animal activists evacuated dogs and cats within 24 hours, while many older people were left in their homes for up to seven days

questions.stem: According to Levy, what did Disney add to its Rapunzel remake, Tangled, that was not in the original Brothers Grimm story?
options: An antiaging theme, with the old witch seeking Rapunzel's hair for eternal youth
A scene in which an older man becomes king

questions.stem: At age seventy-three, after being forced to retire, botanist Ben Duggar isolated which compound that became the world's most widely prescribed antibiotic?
A car manufacturer is debating whether to retire its older assembly-line workers. Based on the Harvard Business School study of a BMW plant, what would you advise?
options: Replace older workers with younger ones to increase speed
Retire everyone over fifty to reduce accidents
Keep age-integrated teams, which increased productivity, reduced absenteeism, and produced fewer defects

questions.stem: A medical school simulates "the aging experience" by giving students blurring glasses, leg weights, and hearing-blocking headsets. What concern does Levy raise about this training?
options: It makes students too sympathetic to older patients
It is too expensive for most medical schools
It does not include enough time in nursing homes
It may reinforce negative stereotypes by leading students to assume older patients will be frail and deficient

questions.stem: Stuck behind a slow car, Sam mutters about "old drivers," then reminds himself that older drivers have fewer accidents and are less likely to text while driving. Which step of Levy's ABC method is he practicing?
options: None; this is an example of age blindness
B: Placing Blame where it is due

questions.stem: A caregiver greets an 88-year-old resident in a loud, singsong voice: "How are we today, sweetie?" According to Levy, what should the caregiver do instead?
options: Address the resident through a family member instead
Speak in normal, everyday language, as she would to a friend her own age
Speak even more slowly and loudly to be sure she is understood

questions.stem: A student wants to build positive age beliefs and plans to model her life on just one role model: an astronaut who flew in space at seventy-seven. What does Levy advise?
options: Avoid role models altogether and rely on willpower
Build a diverse portfolio of positive models, because a single exceptional figure is easily dismissed as an exception
Focus only on that one role model to stay motivated
Choose role models who are younger than she is

questions.stem: At a reunion, someone tells a 70-year-old classmate, "You haven't aged a day!" How would Levy classify this well-intentioned comment?
options: A positive age stereotype that should be encouraged
Age blindness, which can be demeaning because it suggests age identity should be minimized

questions.stem: A senior center wants a simple, evidence-based activity to reduce residents' negative age beliefs. Based on Levy's research, which activity fits best?
options: Journaling once a week for four weeks about an imagined day in the life of a healthy, active older person
Watching popular TV comedies about aging

questions.stem: In their first year, how did the Gray Panthers protest a department store's mandatory retirement policy?
options: They organized a nationwide boycott of the store
They picketed in Santa suits with signs claiming Santa was too old to work there
They held a sit-in at the store's cash registers

questions.stem: A community group gathers older adults to share stories of mistreatment at work and in doctors' offices, and introduces them to the term "ageism" so they recognize it as a societal problem. Which stage of Levy's age liberation movement is this?

An advocacy group meets with advertisers about the health harms of ageist ads and, when talks fail, organizes a boycott of the companies. Which stage of the age liberation movement does this represent?
A group of women holds "Wrinkle Salons" to reclaim wrinkles as signs of hard-won experience rather than something to hide. Levy compares this cultural redefinition to which earlier movement strategy?
options: The civil rights movement's "Black is beautiful" chant
The Stop Hate for Profit Facebook boycott

questions.stem: In the authors' island vaccination thought experiment ($800 budget; $1 per coastal child, $4 per mountain child), how many children are vaccinated under Program A, which vaccinates every child on the coastal plains but none in the mountains?
According to the authors, what is the clear lesson of the vaccination programs thought experiment?
options: Benefit maximization should always override fairness
Fairness should always override benefit maximization
Most people reach consensus on the right program
Fairness and benefit maximization can, and often do, conflict

questions.stem: How do the authors define health care rationing?
options: The selection of individual patients for life-saving treatment
The controlled allocation of scarce health care resources
The denial of care to patients who cannot pay
The government's refusal to fund new medicines

questions.stem: Because there are many more patients than available organs, patients are placed on waiting lists for transplantation. How do the authors characterize these waiting lists?
options: As a purely medical question with no ethical dimension
As an example of disability discrimination

questions.stem: According to the latest data cited by the authors (2019), what percentage of its GDP does the United States spend on health care?
Which of the following is a demographic reason for the scarcity of health care resources described by the authors?
options: Aging societies spend more on health
Patients do not directly bear the costs of their care
Overuse of antibiotics creates resistant bacteria
Medicine can now cure many previously fatal diseases

questions.stem: In 1962, Seattle's Swedish Hospital set up a committee of laypeople to decide which patients would receive a scarce treatment. What was this committee called, and what treatment did it allocate?
The EQ-5D, a widely used questionnaire for describing health states, asks patients to describe how well they function within how many "dimensions" of health?
Using the time trade-off method, if respondents consider 7.6 years in full health just as good as ten years in a particular health state, what is the value of that health state?
Which method for valuing health states asks respondents to choose between living in a health state for a certain amount of time and a risky option with chances of full health or death?
The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) was developed by which international project to measure the harm from mortality and morbidity in populations?
options: The Global Burden of Disease project
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence

questions.stem: Recent updates of the Global Burden of Disease studies include almost how many different diseases and injuries?
What was the most important finding of the web-based surveys, with almost 30,000 respondents, used to evaluate the burden of disabilities for DALYs?
options: Wealthy respondents rated disabilities as far worse than poor respondents
A high degree of agreement in responses across very different social, economic, and cultural backgrounds
Respondents could not compare health states reliably

questions.stem: Program 3 can save 110 people at a cost of $12,100,000. What is its cost-effectiveness ratio?
After policymakers rank interventions by cost-effectiveness into a priority list, what does cost- effectiveness analysis itself NOT tell them?
options: Where the cut-off point (threshold) should be
The cost of each unit of health benefit
How to rank interventions in a priority list
Which interventions are more cost-effective than others

questions.stem: What is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER)?
options: The ratio of an intervention's additional costs to its additional benefits
The cost of one QALY in full health
The rate at which drug prices increase each year
The ratio of total benefits to total costs of all programs

questions.stem: In the late 1980s, the state of Oregon attempted to extend coverage under which program to all potentially eligible residents by limiting the number of services covered?
In 1991, the US federal government rejected the Oregon plan on what basis?
options: It cost more than the state's budget allowed
It violated the Americans with Disabilities Act by discriminating against people with disabilities
It relied on a lottery to select patients

questions.stem: In England and Wales, what term describes inequalities in coverage between different areas caused by decentralized decisions of regional trusts?
In what year was the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (now the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NICE) set up to reduce the effects of the postcode lottery?
Equity weighting of QALYs can be interpreted as an application of which moral view, holding that benefiting a person matters more the worse off that person is?
According to the authors, 1 QALY can represent one year of life in full health, or how many years in a health state whose quality-adjustment factor is 0.5?
The "effectiveness" part of the cost-effectiveness ratio combines which two components?
options: Health-related quality of life and the duration of the intervention's effect
The price of the drug and the number of patients

questions.stem: The authors note that the Americans with Disabilities Act defines disability broadly. Which of the following would fall within this broad characterization?
What does the "disability discrimination objection" to cost-effectiveness analysis claim?
options: Disabilities cannot be measured at all
People with disabilities receive too large a share of health care resources
Cost-effectiveness analysis ignores the cost of interventions
Patients with a limited capacity to benefit from an intervention, such as people with disabilities, will be unfairly disadvantaged

questions.stem: On the extreme version of the social model, how are disabilities understood?
options: As purely medical conditions requiring cure
As conditions that should always receive top priority
As mere differences, with lower quality of life due to the social environment rather than health
As the most severe form of illness

questions.stem: Which argument holds that everyone should be given a chance to have a fair go at a long, complete life, so that priority should go to the young when resources are scarce?
Defenders of the fair innings argument typically argue that giving priority to the young is a matter of what?
options: Cost savings for the health care system

questions.stem: During the COVID-19 pandemic in spring 2020, the Italian Society of Anesthesia, Analgesia, Resuscitation and Intensive Care (SIAARTI) controversially argued that it may be necessary to do what?
options: Use a lottery to allocate ventilators
Give priority to health care workers' families
Set an age limit for ICU admission
Admit patients strictly on a first-come, first-served basis

questions.stem: The Critical Care Society of Southern Africa recommended using age as a "tie-breaker" by sorting patients into life-cycle groups. Which group received priority?
How did the Critical Care Society of Southern Africa justify using life-cycle considerations?
options: People should have equal opportunity to pass through all stages of life
Younger patients are more cost-effective to treat
Older patients are responsible for their own health

questions.stem: The Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society advised that where patients are similarly ranked, which patients should be prioritized?
options: Younger patients who have lived through fewer life stages
Older patients with more life experience
Patients who arrived at the hospital first

questions.stem: In the Oregon Medicaid reform, a list of 709 treatments was drawn up. How many of the top treatments were selected to be provided to all eligible residents?
Which ranking on Oregon's priority list received a lot of attention for seeming counterintuitive?
options: Organ transplants ranked higher than prenatal care
Dental caps for pulp exposure ranked higher than surgical treatment for appendicitis
Cosmetic surgery ranked higher than heart surgery
Cancer drugs ranked higher than vaccinations

questions.stem: The "aggregation thesis" implies which of the following?
options: Every patient should have an equal chance through a lottery
Only the worst-off patient should receive treatment
Benefits to individuals can never be added together
Very small benefits to a great number of people can outweigh far more significant benefits to a few people

questions.stem: In the imaginary "survival lottery" used as an objection to the aggregation thesis, what happens?
options: A randomly selected healthy person's organs are transplanted to save five patients who would otherwise die
Hospitals randomly choose which region receives funding
Patients draw lots to decide who receives a scarce vaccine
The youngest patient is always chosen to survive

questions.stem: When it might be better to target many low-risk individuals, each with small expected benefits, rather than a few high-risk individuals who would greatly benefit, this is known as what?
According to the chapter's further readings, which two philosophers started the philosophical debate on aggregation by rejecting the aggregation thesis?
Which philosophical position captures the intuition that a heart disease patient who chose to smoke should have lower priority than one who did not?
A patient who knowingly chose to smoke and then developed heart disease is described as suffering from what?
According to luck egalitarianism, which inequalities are unjust and should be compensated as a matter of justice?
options: Inequalities that reflect the bad effects of brute luck
Inequalities that reflect the bad effects of option luck

questions.stem: The Whitehall studies, which demonstrated the relationship between socioeconomic status and health, surveyed which population?
What is the "equal access view" regarding the social gradient in health?
options: Wealthier people should pay more for equal access
As long as equal access to health care is secured, there is no further ethical concern about the health gradient
Access to health care should depend on individual responsibility
Everyone should receive exactly the same health outcomes

questions.stem: The US Rare Diseases Act of 2002 defines an orphan disease as one that affects fewer than how many people in the United States?
In 2016, Japan's Chuikyo introduced a "huge seller" repricing rule and urgently cut the price of which high-cost drug by half?
According to the authors, why are antibiotics not an attractive market for pharmaceutical companies?
options: Global on-patent antibiotic sales are only about US$4.7 billion per year, while a single cancer drug can earn twice that
Governments set antibiotic prices above market value
Antibiotics are banned from being patented
Antibiotics are too expensive for patients to buy

questions.stem: Comparing Japan (where the government sets drug prices) and England (where manufacturers set prices freely but NICE applies a cost-effectiveness threshold), what do the authors conclude?
options: Japan does better because the government controls prices
Neither system has any effect on drug prices
England does better than Japan, because rationing based on cost-effectiveness helps induce an acceptable range of drug prices

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four factors the authors list that can influence drug prices?
options: The number of physicians in a country

questions.stem: According to the authors, if there were no attempt to control the allocation of health care resources, who would end up rationing care?
options: No one, because scarcity would disappear
Patients themselves through the free market
Frontline health care workers, at their own judgment and without general guidelines

questions.stem: Why do the authors argue that the principles for allocating health care resources cannot simply be decided by a vote?
options: Moral justification is not a majoritarian procedure
Voting is too expensive to organize
Citizens do not care about health care

questions.stem: What name do the authors give to the relatively new area of philosophy that addresses questions arising at the population level, such as the allocation of health care resources?
According to the authors, what are most real-world examples of health care rationing like?
options: Rare events that occur only during pandemics
Mundane and uncontroversial, such as setting subsidy levels for pharmaceuticals and co-payments
Decisions made only in low-income countries
Dramatic life-and-death choices between individual patients

questions.stem: In the vaccination thought experiment, a student who chooses Program B (half the coastal children and half the mountain children) most likely does so because of which consideration?
options: Benefit maximization: Program B vaccinates more children
Fairness: it is wrong to exclude children merely because they live in a remote place
Efficiency: Program B is easier to deliver

questions.stem: In the authors' experience, students who favored Program A in the first vaccination question overwhelmingly choose which program in the follow-up question?
options: Program E, vaccinating the remaining half of both groups
Program C, vaccinating all the mountain children against the first disease
Program D, vaccinating the coastal children against a second disease
Program F, vaccinating the coastal children against the second disease

questions.stem: The WHO and UNAIDS "3 by 5" program aimed to provide antiretroviral therapy to three million people by the end of 2005. When was the target actually met?

A state government decides to build a new specialist hospital in City X rather than City Y, and an insurer raises co-payments for MRI scans. According to the authors' definition, these decisions are examples of what?
options: Neither is rationing, because no individual patient is denied care
Only the insurance decision is rationing
Only the hospital decision is rationing
Health care rationing, because both are controlled allocations of scarce health care resources

questions.stem: According to the authors, almost how many people in the United States (about 9 percent of the population) had no health insurance as of 2019?
What attitude do the authors say most people hold about inequalities in health compared with inequalities in income?
options: People view both as equally acceptable
People are more tolerant of health inequalities than income inequalities
People believe health inequalities reflect differences in effort
People are generally more tolerant of income inequalities than of inequalities in health and access to health care

questions.stem: A benevolent dictator spends enough to meet every medical need and eliminates all inefficiencies. According to the authors, why would rationing still be necessary?
options: Rationing would no longer be necessary in this situation
Choices must still be made about what to offer first, since time is a scarce resource and better services can create new scarcity
Doctors would refuse to work without rationing

questions.stem: In the God Committee transcript, which concern did committee members raise about the candidate who was a housewife from Walla Walla?
options: She was too old to benefit from dialysis
She could not commute for treatment, and her husband lacked the funds to move the family to Seattle
She did not have health insurance

questions.stem: Using the time trade-off method, a patient says that 6 years in full health is just as good as 10 years living with chronic back pain. What value does this assign to the back-pain health state?

In a standard gamble, a respondent is indifferent between living with a condition for certain and a treatment with an 80 percent chance of full health and a 20 percent chance of immediate death. What value does this assign to the condition?
What criticism of the standard gamble method do the authors mention?
options: It can be time consuming to explain and administer, and participants may find it hard to understand
It can only be used for children
It does not produce numbers that can be compared

questions.stem: A patient facing a decision about a risky surgery must weigh the chance of a cure against the risk of death. Why do the authors suggest the standard gamble may be more adequate than a simple rating scale for valuing health states?
options: Because real patients sometimes must make treatment gambles and trade-offs between health states, which the standard gamble mirrors
Because the standard gamble does not require any choices
Because the rating scale always produces higher values
Because the standard gamble is faster to administer

questions.stem: A ministry of health wants to measure how much harm malaria, HIV, and road injuries cause in its population, rather than the benefit of a specific treatment. Which measure was designed for this purpose?
options: DALYs, which represent the gap between actual health and an ideal level of health
QALYs, which measure the benefit of interventions

questions.stem: Anemia can be caused by malaria, maternal hemorrhaging, or peptic ulcer disease. How do the authors say the Global Burden of Disease handles these different causes?
options: Only anemia caused by malaria is counted
Each must receive a completely different disability weight
They are separate conditions but can share a common disability weight because they lead to the same health outcome
Anemia is excluded from the Global Burden of Disease

questions.stem: With the same $10 million budget, Program X saves 100 lives and Program Y saves 50 lives. If the goal is to maximize health benefits, which is true?
options: Program Y has the more favorable ratio because it costs more per life
Cost-effectiveness cannot compare programs that save lives
Program X has the more favorable (lower) cost-effectiveness ratio and should be preferred

questions.stem: A health system implements Program 1 and has $2,100,000 left. Program 3 saves additional people at $110,000 each. About how many additional people can be saved with the remaining money?
A new cancer drug costs $30,000 more than the current treatment and produces 1.5 more QALYs. What is its incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER)?
A health agency has set a cost-effectiveness threshold of $50,000 per QALY. A new therapy has an ICER of $80,000 per QALY. How would the therapy be classified?
options: Impossible to classify without knowing the patient's age
Below the cut-off on the priority list: not cost-effective and given lower priority
Above the cut-off: cost-effective and good value for money
Automatically covered, because all new therapies are covered

questions.stem: Who made up the Oregon Health Services Commission created to develop the priority list of health services?
options: Five primary care physicians, a public health nurse, a social worker, and four representatives of the public
Five state legislators and five hospital administrators
Ten health economists and a medical ethicist
Representatives of pharmaceutical and insurance companies

questions.stem: Under the English "postcode lottery," some trusts used to spend about how much more on cancer care than others?

Two patients would each gain 2 QALYs from treatment, but Patient A is much worse off in health than Patient B. A policymaker applies equity weights that count A's QALYs more heavily. Which moral view does this reflect?
Treatment A gives a patient 5 years at a quality-adjustment factor of 0.8. Treatment B gives 8 years at 0.4. Which produces more QALYs?
options: They produce exactly the same number of QALYs
QALYs cannot be calculated from this information

questions.stem: Two patients need the same life-saving treatment. One uses a wheelchair due to paraplegia, so the QALYs gained from saving that patient's life are calculated as lower. Critics would say this illustrates which objection?
In a discussion question, the authors note that some countries cover prenatal genetic tests even though most parents terminate pregnancies when a disorder is detected. Which countries are named?
options: The United States, Mexico, and Brazil
Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Scandinavian countries, and some provinces of Canada

questions.stem: Two equal groups need different life-saving treatments with identical benefits; the only difference is that one group is 20 years old and the other is 70. A defender of the fair innings argument would give priority to whom, and why?
options: The 70-year-olds, because they are worse off in health
The 20-year-olds, because everyone should have a fair chance at a long, complete life
Neither, because a lottery must decide
The 70-year-olds, because they have contributed more to society

questions.stem: Under the Critical Care Society of Southern Africa's guidelines, two ICU candidates are in the same priority group: a 35-year-old and a 68-year-old. Who would receive priority under the tie-breaker?
options: Neither; a lottery must be used
The 68-year-old, who has more medical need
The 35-year-old, who is in an earlier life-cycle group
Whoever arrived at the hospital first

questions.stem: Under the Southern Africa guidelines, patients in all priority groups had to have a Clinical Frailty Score at or below what number?
An ICU guideline says age is used "only as a tie-breaker." Why do the authors call this description somewhat misleading?
options: When beds are limited and many patients have similar prognoses, the tie-breaker can end up deciding many admissions, so age plays a major role
Because age is always the first criterion considered
Because tie-breakers are illegal in most countries
Because age is never actually used in practice

questions.stem: The 2026-27 debate topic proposes allocating limited resources to "patients with the greatest likelihood of long-term survival." This most directly emphasizes which component of measuring health benefits in cost-effectiveness analysis?
options: The duration of the intervention's effect, measured in life years
The patient's responsibility for their condition

questions.stem: A health system could either save one patient's life or relieve mild headaches for one million people. Someone who accepts the aggregation thesis would say what?
options: A lottery must decide between the options
The benefits cannot be compared at all
The one life must always be saved, no matter how many headaches
The small benefits to a very large number of people can outweigh the significant benefit to one person

questions.stem: A government chooses a population-wide salt-reduction campaign, giving small expected benefits to millions, over intensive treatment of a few high-risk patients. Which concept does this illustrate?
Besides general preventive policy, which examples do the authors give of where the prevention paradox arises?
options: Fluoridation of the water supply and antenatal screening programs

questions.stem: According to the chapter's further readings, which philosopher introduced prioritarianism?
According to the further readings, the "principle of pairwise comparison" was put forward by whom?

Patient A developed heart disease from a rare genetic condition. Patient B developed heart disease after a lifetime of heavy smoking despite knowing the risks. Under luck egalitarianism, how should their situations be classified?
options: A suffered bad brute luck (to be compensated); B suffered bad option luck (not unjust)
A suffered bad option luck; B suffered bad brute luck
Both suffered bad option luck and neither should be compensated
Both suffered bad brute luck and should be treated equally

questions.stem: A recreational skydiver who knowingly takes risks is injured. A luck egalitarian would most likely argue what about the resulting inequality?
options: It reflects bad option luck and is not unjust, so it need not be compensated as a matter of justice
It should be decided by a lottery
It is part of the social gradient in health
It reflects bad brute luck and must be fully compensated

questions.stem: The first Whitehall study, which began in 1967, surveyed approximately how many male civil servants?
A country guarantees universal, equal access to health care, yet low-income citizens still die years earlier than wealthy citizens. A proponent of the equal access view would say what?
options: The poor are responsible for their own worse health
Health care access should be rationed by income
There is no further ethical concern, since equal access to health care has been secured
The government must equalize incomes immediately

questions.stem: Besides health care, which factors do the authors list as contributing to people's health in the discussion of the social gradient?
options: Income, education, sanitation, air quality, and housing
Only access to doctors and hospitals

questions.stem: In Japan, which body makes the recommendations that the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare uses to set drug prices?
options: The Central Social Insurance Medical Council (Chuikyo)

questions.stem: A company releases a new drug that is only slightly more effective than an existing one. According to the authors, which pricing factor limits how high it can set the price?
options: The price of related drugs taken together

questions.stem: A manufacturer knows no competitor can produce a similar drug for many years, so it sets a very high price. Which pricing factor is at work?
options: Market competition (or the lack of it)

questions.stem: A rare disease affects about 150,000 people in the United States. Under the US Rare Diseases Act of 2002, how would it be classified?
options: As a common disease, since it affects more than 100,000 people
It cannot be classified without European Union approval
As an orphan disease only if it is fatal
As an orphan disease, since it affects fewer than 200,000 people

questions.stem: Japan's 2016 "huge seller" repricing rule applies a 50 percent price cut to drugs whose annual sales exceed what amount?
According to the authors, where are most generic manufacturers of off-patent antibiotics located?
A hospital has no guidelines for allocating scarce ICU beds, so each doctor decides at the bedside. Which problems do the authors predict?
options: Perfectly fair outcomes, since doctors know their patients best
Lower costs with no ethical problems
Unfairness, lack of transparency, and arbitrary decisions open to mistakes, prejudice, and corruption

questions.stem: To what do the authors contrast health care to show that it is not an ordinary market good?
A legislature proposes letting politicians decide all rationing priorities directly. Based on the authors' reasoning, why might it be better to delegate these decisions to an agency like NICE?
options: Politicians are not allowed to discuss health care
Such agencies are more removed from electoral pressures and powerful interest groups
Agencies do not need ethical principles
